prompt: The lesson keeps the paid orders with **Equals** `paid` rather than removing the `cancelled` ones. What does that choice protect against?
hint: Think of a status the platform has not invented yet.

choices.text: Nothing; the two filters give the same rows on every file
choices.why: They agree only while `paid` and `cancelled` are the only statuses.

choices.text: A new status such as `refunded`, which would slip in
choices.why: Right. Keeping what you want leaves out anything you did not foresee.

choices.text: Codes in lower case, which the Equals filter also corrects
choices.why: The filter looks at `Status` only. The codes are section 02's second step.

choices.text: A refresh that fails when a month has no cancelled orders
choices.why: A filter that matches nothing simply removes nothing; it does not fail.

prompt: How many rows does `WebOrders` keep after the filter on `Status`?
hint: Two of the 24 orders were cancelled.

prompt: You add a custom column `Revenue` with `[Bags] * [Price]`. What is left to do?
hint: Look at the icon at the left of its header.

choices.text: Nothing, since a custom column takes the type of its formula
choices.why: A custom column is created with no type; the icon shows it, and loading it untyped invites trouble.

choices.text: Copy the formula down to the last row
choices.why: A custom column is computed once per row by itself; there is no filling down.

choices.text: Wrap the formula in `SUM` so it totals
choices.why: The column is one value per row. Totals come later, with Group By or a pivot table.

choices.text: Set its type, Decimal Number
choices.why: Right. The type follows as a step of its own.

prompt: In a custom column's formula, a column of the same row is written between square ___, as in `[Bags] * [Price]`.
hint: The characters around the name.

prompt: An export from a till writes `2026-08-15 14:30` in its date column. What turns that column into plain days in Power Query?
hint: One of the steps in the lesson's last table.

choices.text: Setting the column's type to Date
choices.why: Right. The time of day is dropped and the day stays.

choices.text: Trim, which removes the characters after the space
choices.why: Trim removes spaces at the ends of a text, not part of a value.

choices.text: Remove Duplicates on the column
choices.why: That removes repeated rows; every value keeps its time.

choices.text: Fill Down, which copies the day into the time
choices.why: Fill Down copies values into empty cells below them; it does not touch a time.

prompt: In `WebMargin`, what is the total `Margin`, `[Revenue] - [Bags] * [Unit cost]`, of the 22 paid orders, in reais?
hint: Revenue R$ 3,125.50, less what the coffee cost.

prompt: You merge `WebOrders` with `Products` before making the codes upper case. What does the dialog report?
hint: `dec250` and `mog250` are still in lower case.

choices.text: 22 of 22 rows, because a merge ignores case as XLOOKUP does
choices.why: That is the difference the lesson stresses: XLOOKUP ignores case, a merge does not.

choices.text: An error, because the key holds mixed case
choices.why: Nothing fails. The two orders simply get an empty `Unit cost`.

choices.text: 20 of 22 rows: orders `W2010` and `W2019` find no product at all
choices.why: Right. A merge compares text exactly, capitals included, so `dec250` is not `DEC250`.

choices.text: 24 of 24 rows, since the filter has not run yet
choices.why: The merge is made after the filter here; the question is only about case.

prompt: Match each join kind to the rows it keeps.
hint: Outer keeps, Inner requires, Anti looks for what is missing.

pairs.right: Every row of the first, with matches where there are any
Only rows that match on both sides
Rows of the first with no match
Rows of the second with no match

right_distractors: Every row of the first, each exactly once whatever matches

prompt: A Left Outer merge of the 22 paid orders with `Freight` returns 23 rows. What made the extra one?
hint: Count the rows each order finds on the right.

choices.text: A cancelled order that came back through the merge
choices.why: The cancelled orders were filtered out before the merge, and a merge adds no rows from the first table.

choices.text: The three collected orders, which Left Outer counts twice
choices.why: They appear once each, with an empty freight.

choices.text: The header row of the courier's file
choices.why: The header became column names in lesson 13; it is not a row.

choices.text: Order `W2014`, which has two freight rows
choices.why: Right. A merge brings every matching row, so a repeated key on the right repeats the row on the left.

prompt: How many rows does a **Left Anti** merge of `WebOrders` (22 paid orders) with `Freight` on `Order` return?
hint: The orders nobody shipped.

prompt: Which question does a Right Anti merge of `WebOrders` with `Freight` answer?
hint: Rows of the second table with no partner in the first.

choices.text: Which orders were collected at the roastery
choices.why: Those are orders with no freight row: rows of the first with no match, a Left Anti.

choices.text: Which invoice lines are for orders the shop has no record of
choices.why: Right. This quarter there are none, and next quarter this join is how you would find one.

choices.text: Which orders were shipped more than once
choices.why: Repeated keys show up as extra rows in a Left Outer merge, not in an anti join.

choices.text: Which products cost more to ship than they earned
choices.why: That needs both tables' values compared row by row, not a join kind.

prompt: Appending `WebOrders` straight under `Sales` gives 130 rows and nine columns. Why nine?
hint: Compare the two queries' column names.

choices.text: `Order` and `Sale` differ, so each becomes a column
choices.why: Right, and `Customer` and `Channel` are empty on the web rows for the same reason.

choices.text: Append adds a column saying which query each row came from
choices.why: That is From Folder's `Source.Name`; an append adds no column of its own.

choices.text: The two queries list their columns in different orders
choices.why: Order does not matter to an append; names do.

choices.text: `Revenue` is a number in one and text in the other
choices.why: Types do not split a column; only names do.

prompt: What is the total `Revenue` of `AllSales`, `Sales` with the paid web orders appended, in reais?
hint: R$ 51,494 plus the web shop's quarter.

prompt: How does an append decide which column of the second query goes under which column of the first?
hint: Section 04's first attempt shows it.

choices.text: By position: first under first, second under second
choices.why: Then reordering the columns of `WebAsSales` would have mattered, and it did not.

choices.text: By type: numbers under numbers, text under text
choices.why: Types play no part in lining columns up.

choices.text: By name, and only by name
choices.why: Right. Same name, one column; a name on one side only becomes a column of its own.

choices.text: By asking you to pair them in a dialog
choices.why: No dialog pairs columns; that is why names have to agree beforehand.

prompt: Why does the lesson rename `Order` to `Sale` in a new query made with **Reference**, rather than inside `WebOrders`?
hint: Who else reads `WebOrders`?

choices.text: So `WebOrders` keeps its names for the queries that read it
choices.why: Right. A reference starts from `WebOrders` as it is after its last step, and adds its own steps.

choices.text: Reference queries refresh faster than the queries they read
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; what other queries expect is.

choices.text: A query made from a folder cannot be renamed
choices.why: Its columns can be renamed like any other; section 02 did exactly that.

choices.text: Because `Sales` cannot be appended to a query loaded as a table
choices.why: Any two queries can be appended; the loading does not matter.

prompt: How many rows does `Budget` hold after **Unpivot Other Columns**?
hint: Channels times months.

prompt: Next year the budget arrives with columns `2027-01` to `2027-12`. You point the query at the new file. Which unpivot keeps working, and why?
hint: What does each command write into the step?

choices.text: Both, because Power Query renames months automatically
choices.why: Nothing renames them; the difference is what each step names.

choices.text: Unpivot Only Selected Columns, because it lists the months it found
choices.why: It lists 2026's months by name, so 2027's are left alone.

choices.text: Neither: a new year always needs a new query
choices.why: The point of Other Columns is that it does not.

choices.text: Unpivot Other Columns, because the step names only `Channel`
choices.why: Right. Everything that is not `Channel` is unpivoted, whatever the months are called.

prompt: Put the steps of the `Budget` query in order.
hint: Each step needs what the one before it made.
items: Promote the first line to headers
Rename Attribute to Month and Value to Budget
Set Month to Date and Budget to Whole Number
trap: Setting Month to Date before adding the suffix asks for a date from `2026-03`, which is not a whole date.

prompt: Why can a pivot table not filter the budget file by month as it arrives?
hint: Where is the month in the wide file?

choices.text: Pivot tables cannot read data imported from a CSV file
choices.why: They can, through a query; the problem is the shape.

choices.text: The months are text and a filter needs dates
choices.why: A pivot table filters text happily; the months are not in a column at all.

choices.text: The month is a column name, not a value in any cell
choices.why: Right. A filter chooses among values, and `2026-03` is nowhere in the data.

choices.text: Twelve columns are more than a pivot table allows
choices.why: A pivot table takes far more columns than that; each would just be a separate field.

prompt: In `BudgetVsActual`, what is the `Variance` of `Online` for January to June 2026, in reais?
hint: Revenue minus budget; the web shop did well.

prompt: When is Group By the better tool than a pivot table?
hint: What can happen to a query's result that cannot happen to a pivot table?

choices.text: When somebody will drag fields around to explore the totals
choices.why: That is what a pivot table is for, lessons 10 and 11.

choices.text: When the summary feeds another step, such as a merge
choices.why: Right. A grouped query is an input; a pivot table is the end of the line.

choices.text: Whenever the data has more than one column to total
choices.why: Both total several columns; the choice is about what comes next.

choices.text: Only when the source is a CSV file and not a table
choices.why: Group By works on any query, from any source.

prompt: Before merging `Freight` into `WebOrders`, what makes the merge return one row per order?
hint: The repeated key is on the right side.

choices.text: Remove Duplicates on `Freight`, keeping the first row of `W2014`
choices.why: That drops the cost of the second parcel; the freight total would be short by R$ 31.20.

choices.text: Grouping `Freight` by `Order` with the Sum of `Freight`
choices.why: Right. 19 rows, one per order, both parcels of `W2014` added together, and the merge gives 22 rows.

choices.text: Choosing Inner instead of Left Outer
choices.why: An inner join still repeats `W2014`, and also drops the three collected orders.

choices.text: Filtering `W2014` out of `WebOrders`
choices.why: That hides a real paid order to make the count look right.

prompt: `WebByProduct` groups `WebOrders` by `Product`. Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: A grouped query is still a query.

choices.text: It has 6 rows, one per product
choices.why: Six codes remain once section 02 made them upper case.

choices.text: It sees the rows after the filter on `Status`
choices.why: It reads `WebOrders` after its last step, so the cancelled orders are not counted.

choices.text: It changes when `WebOrders` changes and the workbook is refreshed
choices.why: A reference follows its source on every refresh.

choices.text: You can drag its fields around like a pivot table's
choices.why: Its result is a fixed table; rearranging totals by dragging is what a pivot table does.

prompt: A refresh stops with `Expression.Error: The column 'Qty' of the table wasn't found.` What happened?
hint: Read the message literally.

choices.text: The file is missing from the `web` folder
choices.why: A missing file gives an error naming the path, not a column.

choices.text: The column is there but holds text instead of numbers
choices.why: Wrong types give errors in cells, not a missing column.

choices.text: Power Query cannot read more than three files
choices.why: From Folder reads as many files as the folder holds.

choices.text: A step names `Qty`, which the source no longer has
choices.why: Right. A platform renaming `Qty` to `Quantity` is the usual cause; a rename inserted before the failing step repairs it.

prompt: You delete the `Renamed Columns` step of `WebOrders`. What happens to the custom column `Revenue`?
hint: Its formula is `[Bags] * [Price]`.

choices.text: Every row of it becomes an error
choices.why: Right. `Bags` and `Price` no longer exist under those names, so the formula has nothing to read.

choices.text: It keeps its values, because they were computed when it was made
choices.why: A query recomputes every step on every run; nothing is kept from earlier.

choices.text: Power Query renames the columns back on its own
choices.why: Nothing renames them; the step that did is gone.

choices.text: The step is moved to the end of the list
choices.why: Deleting removes a step; it does not move the others.

prompt: Before deleting the `Budget` query, where do you see which queries read it?
hint: A view in the editor draws the arrows.

choices.text: In the Advanced Editor of `Budget` itself
choices.why: A query's code names what it reads, not what reads it.

choices.text: In **Data › Get Data › Data Source Settings**
choices.why: That lists files and servers, not the queries built on each other.

choices.text: In **View › Query Dependencies**
choices.why: Right. Anything with an arrow from `Budget` would break.

choices.text: Nowhere: Excel deletes the dependent queries with it
choices.why: It does not; they are left to fail at the next refresh.

prompt: Each of these does two steps in the wrong order. Match it to what you get.
hint: The table of section 07.

pairs.left: Merge with `Products`, then uppercase the codes
Group by product, then keep the paid orders
Multiply `Price` by `Bags`, then set `Price` to a number

right_distractors: The CSV file rewritten with the new order

prompt: Put the work behind `BudgetVsActual` in order, from the budget file to the variance.
hint: A month can only be filtered once it is a value.
items: Unpivot the budget's months into rows
Group by channel, summing the budget
Merge with the actual revenue by channel
trap: Grouping before keeping January to June would compare a whole year's budget with half a year of sales.

prompt: A supplier sends a price list with one row per month and one column per product: `Month`, `SUL250`, `CER1K`, and so on. You want one row per product per month. What do you do?
hint: Which column should stay as it is?

choices.text: Select every product column and choose Pivot Column
choices.why: Pivot goes the other way, from rows to columns.

choices.text: Group by `Month`, summing every product column
choices.why: That keeps one row per month; the products stay across.

choices.text: Append the file to itself once per product
choices.why: Appending stacks copies; it does not turn columns into rows.

choices.text: Select `Month` alone and choose Unpivot Other Columns
choices.why: Right. `Month` stays; every product column becomes rows, and a new product next month is unpivoted too.
